meta.title: Subject-Verb Agreement Test
meta.description: A comprehensive 30-question test covering singular/plural subject-verb agreement, compound subjects (and, or, nor), indefinite pronouns, collective nouns, and subjects with intervening phrases.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'The number', which is singular. The phrase 'of applicants who have applied for the position' modifies 'number' but does not change its grammatical number. Therefore, 'have since' must be corrected to 'has since' or simply 'has'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'The number of' is followed by a singular verb, while 'a number of' is followed by a plural verb.

rules.title: 1. The number of + plural noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: The head noun is 'number', so the verb is singular.
rules.structure: The number of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: The number of applicants has risen.
The number of cars is increasing.

rules.title: 2. A number of + plural noun + plural verb
rules.explanation: 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb.
rules.structure: A number of + plural noun + plural verb
notes: A number of applicants have applied.
A number of issues remain.

common_mistakes.wrong: The number of applicants have risen.
common_mistakes.correct: The number of applicants has risen.

other_examples.sentence: The number of complaints has decreased.
A number of complaints have been received.

details_explanation.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'The technicians' is plural and closer to the verb, so 'was' must become 'were' (or 'were all').
details_explanation.introduction: In 'neither ... nor' constructions, the verb follows the proximity rule: it agrees with the subject closest to it.

rules.title: 1. Proximity rule
rules.explanation: The verb matches the number of the nearest subject.
rules.structure: Neither S1 nor S2 + verb (agrees with S2)
notes: Neither the engineer nor the technicians were aware.
Neither the technicians nor the engineer was aware.

rules.title: 2. Avoid ambiguity
rules.explanation: Place the plural subject closer to the verb if a plural verb sounds more natural, or rephrase the sentence.
rules.structure: Either reorder subjects or use a plural verb with the nearer plural subject
notes: Neither the manager nor the employees were informed.
Neither the employees nor the manager was informed.

common_mistakes.wrong: Neither the engineer nor the technicians was aware.
common_mistakes.correct: Neither the engineer nor the technicians were aware.

other_examples.sentence: Neither the captain nor the players were satisfied.
other_examples.translation: Baik kapten maupun para pemain tidak puas.

other_examples.sentence: Neither the players nor the captain was satisfied.
other_examples.translation: Baik para pemain maupun kapten tidak puas.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Each' is an indefinite pronoun and is grammatically singular, even when followed by 'of + plural noun'. The correct verb is 'has been required' or 'is required'.
details_explanation.introduction: Indefinite pronouns such as 'each', 'everyone', 'everybody', 'someone', and 'nobody' take singular verbs.

rules.title: 1. Each of + plural noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: The subject is 'each', not the plural noun after 'of'.
rules.structure: Each of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: Each of the managers has been trained.
Each of the students is responsible.

rules.title: 2. Each + singular noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: When 'each' directly modifies a singular noun, the subject is also singular.
rules.structure: Each + singular noun + singular verb
notes: Each manager has a key.
Each applicant is interviewed separately.

common_mistakes.wrong: Each of the managers have been informed.
common_mistakes.correct: Each of the managers has been informed.

other_examples.sentence: Each of the rooms has its own bathroom.
other_examples.translation: Setiap kamar memiliki kamar mandinya sendiri.

other_examples.sentence: Each candidate is required to submit a form.

details_explanation.explanation: The collective noun 'committee' is treated as singular when it acts as a single unit. Therefore, 'have been unable' should be 'has been unable' or 'is unable'.
details_explanation.introduction: Collective nouns such as 'committee', 'team', 'family', 'government', and 'audience' are usually singular in American English when the group acts as one entity.

rules.title: 1. Collective noun as a unit
rules.explanation: Use a singular verb when the group acts together.
rules.structure: Collective noun + singular verb
notes: The committee has decided.
The team is winning.

rules.title: 2. British English variation
rules.explanation: In British English, collective nouns may take plural verbs when members act individually, but American English strongly prefers singular verbs.
rules.structure: Collective noun + plural verb (British, individual action)
notes: The committee have disagreed among themselves. (British)
The committee has decided. (American)

common_mistakes.wrong: The committee have reached a decision.
common_mistakes.correct: The committee has reached a decision.
common_mistakes.reason: The committee acts as one unit.

other_examples.sentence: The committee has approved the budget.
The audience was impressed by the performance.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'The bouquet' (singular). The phrase 'along with the handwritten card' is an intervening phrase and does not make the subject plural. The verb should be 'was delivered' or 'has been delivered'.
details_explanation.introduction: Phrases such as 'along with', 'together with', 'as well as', and 'in addition to' do not change the number of the subject.

rules.title: 1. Intervening phrases do not affect the subject
rules.explanation: Remove the phrase to identify the true subject.
rules.structure: Subject + along with/together with + noun + verb (agrees with subject)
notes: The bouquet was delivered. (correct)
The bouquet along with the card was delivered.

rules.title: 2. Difference from 'and'
rules.explanation: 'And' creates a compound plural subject; 'along with' does not.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 = plural; S1 along with S2 = agrees with S1
notes: The bouquet and the card were delivered. (plural)
The bouquet along with the card was delivered. (singular)

common_mistakes.wrong: The bouquet along with the card were delivered.
common_mistakes.correct: The bouquet along with the card was delivered.

other_examples.sentence: The CEO, along with the directors, was present.
The students, together with the teacher, are going on a trip.
other_examples.translation: Para siswa, bersama guru, pergi dalam perjalanan.

details_explanation.explanation: With 'not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. 'The workers' is plural and nearer, so 'was informed' should be 'were informed' or 'were all informed'.
details_explanation.introduction: Correlative conjunctions such as 'not only ... but also', 'either ... or', and 'neither ... nor' follow the proximity rule.

rules.title: 1. Proximity rule with correlative conjunctions
rules.explanation: The verb agrees with the nearest subject.
rules.structure: Not only S1 but also S2 + verb (agrees with S2)
notes: Not only the manager but also the employees were informed.
Not only the employees but also the manager was informed.

rules.title: 2. Parallel structure
rules.explanation: Keep the grammatical forms after each conjunction parallel.
rules.structure: Not only + noun + but also + noun
notes: Not only the supervisor but also the workers were informed.

common_mistakes.wrong: Not only the supervisor but also the workers was informed.
common_mistakes.correct: Not only the supervisor but also the workers were informed.

details_explanation.explanation: With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. 'The certified copy' is singular and closer, so 'are required' should be 'is required' or 'will be required'.
details_explanation.introduction: In 'either ... or' and 'neither ... nor' constructions, the verb agrees with the subject closest to it.

rules.title: 1. Singular nearer subject
rules.explanation: If the second subject is singular, use a singular verb.
rules.structure: Either plural S1 or singular S2 + singular verb
notes: Either the documents or the copy is required.
Either the students or the teacher is responsible.

rules.title: 2. Plural nearer subject
rules.explanation: If the second subject is plural, use a plural verb.
rules.structure: Either singular S1 or plural S2 + plural verb
notes: Either the copy or the documents are required.
Either the teacher or the students are responsible.

common_mistakes.wrong: Either the documents or the copy are required.
common_mistakes.correct: Either the documents or the copy is required.

other_examples.translation: Entah manajer atau para asisten tersedia.

details_explanation.explanation: 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb. The subject is effectively 'complaints', so 'has been filed' should be 'have been filed' or 'were filed'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'A number of' is different from 'the number of'. 'A number of' is followed by a plural verb.

rules.title: 1. A number of + plural noun + plural verb
rules.explanation: 'A number of' functions like 'several'.
rules.structure: A number of + plural noun + plural verb
notes: A number of complaints have been filed.
A number of students are absent.

rules.title: 2. The number of + plural noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: 'The number of' focuses on the number itself.
rules.structure: The number of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: The number of complaints has increased.
The number of students is rising.

common_mistakes.wrong: A number of complaints has been filed.
common_mistakes.correct: A number of complaints have been filed.
common_mistakes.reason: 'A number of' takes a plural verb.

other_examples.sentence: A number of issues have arisen.

details_explanation.explanation: 'The majority of' can take a singular or plural verb depending on the noun after 'of'. Here, 'evidence' is uncountable/singular, so the verb should be 'supports' or 'has supported'.
details_explanation.introduction: Expressions like 'the majority of', 'most of', and 'some of' agree with the noun that follows 'of'.

rules.title: 1. Majority of + uncountable noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: Uncountable nouns take singular verbs.
rules.structure: The majority of + uncountable noun + singular verb
notes: The majority of the evidence supports the theory.
The majority of the water is polluted.

rules.title: 2. Majority of + plural noun + plural verb
rules.explanation: Plural nouns take plural verbs.
rules.structure: The majority of + plural noun + plural verb
notes: The majority of voters support the plan.
The majority of students are present.

common_mistakes.wrong: The majority of the evidence support the claim.
common_mistakes.correct: The majority of the evidence supports the claim.

other_examples.sentence: The majority of the information is accurate.
The majority of the employees are satisfied.

details_explanation.explanation: 'More than one' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb. Therefore, 'have expressed' should be 'has expressed' or simply 'expressed'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'More than one' is treated as singular even though it suggests plurality.

rules.title: 1. More than one + singular noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: The verb is singular.
rules.structure: More than one + singular noun + singular verb
notes: More than one candidate has expressed reservations.
More than one student is absent.

rules.title: 2. More than two/three + plural noun + plural verb
rules.explanation: With numbers greater than one, use plural nouns and verbs.
rules.structure: More than two + plural noun + plural verb
notes: More than two candidates have applied.
More than three issues remain.

common_mistakes.wrong: More than one candidate have applied.
common_mistakes.correct: More than one candidate has applied.
common_mistakes.reason: 'More than one' takes a singular verb.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and takes a singular verb. Thus, 'have underestimated' should be 'has underestimated' or 'underestimated'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Many a' is a literary or formal expression meaning 'many', but grammatically it is singular.

rules.title: 1. Many a + singular noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: The verb agrees with the singular noun.
rules.structure: Many a + singular noun + singular verb
notes: Many a student has underestimated the exam.
Many a worker is affected.

rules.title: 2. Many + plural noun + plural verb
rules.explanation: Without 'a', 'many' takes a plural noun and plural verb.
rules.structure: Many + plural noun + plural verb
notes: Many students have underestimated the exam.
Many workers are affected.

common_mistakes.wrong: Many a student have failed the test.
common_mistakes.correct: Many a student has failed the test.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Criteria' is the plural of 'criterion' and takes a plural verb. The correct verb is 'were revised' or 'have been revised'.
details_explanation.introduction: Some nouns retain Latin or Greek plural forms, such as 'criteria', 'phenomena', and 'analyses'. These are plural and take plural verbs.

rules.title: 1. Criteria is plural
rules.explanation: Use a plural verb with 'criteria'.
rules.structure: Criteria + plural verb
notes: The criteria were revised.
The criteria have changed.

rules.title: 2. Criterion is singular
rules.explanation: Use a singular verb with 'criterion'.
rules.structure: Criterion + singular verb
notes: The criterion was revised.
One criterion is essential.

common_mistakes.wrong: The criteria was clear.
common_mistakes.correct: The criteria were clear.

other_examples.sentence: The criteria for admission are strict.
The main criterion is academic performance.

details_explanation.explanation: 'The police' is always plural in English and requires a plural verb. Therefore, 'has confirmed' should be 'have confirmed' or 'confirmed'.
details_explanation.introduction: Some nouns are always plural, including 'police', 'people', 'cattle', and 'clergy'.

rules.title: 1. Police takes a plural verb
rules.explanation: 'Police' refers to members of a police force collectively but is grammatically plural.
rules.structure: The police + plural verb
notes: The police have arrived.
The police are investigating.

rules.title: 2. Do not use 'police is'
rules.explanation: Avoid singular verbs with 'police'.
rules.structure: Incorrect: The police is ...
notes: Incorrect: The police is coming.
Correct: The police are coming.

common_mistakes.wrong: The police has arrested the suspect.
common_mistakes.correct: The police have arrested the suspect.

other_examples.sentence: The police are questioning the witnesses.

details_explanation.explanation: In 'one of the few employees who ...', the relative pronoun 'who' refers to 'employees', which is plural, so the verb in the relative clause should be 'have access' or 'had access'. The main verb 'was unavailable' correctly agrees with 'One'.
details_explanation.introduction: In 'one of the + plural noun + who/that ...', the relative clause verb usually agrees with the plural noun.

rules.title: 1. Relative clause agrees with plural noun
rules.explanation: 'Who' refers to the plural noun after 'of'.
rules.structure: One of the + plural noun + who + plural verb
notes: One of the employees who have access was absent.
She is one of the few people who know the truth.

rules.title: 2. Main verb agrees with 'one'
rules.explanation: The main clause subject is 'one', which is singular.
rules.structure: One of the + plural noun + singular main verb
notes: One of the employees was absent.
One of the students is missing.

common_mistakes.wrong: One of the employees who has access was absent.
common_mistakes.correct: One of the employees who have access was absent.

details_explanation.explanation: In 'There is/are ...', the verb agrees with the noun phrase that follows. 'A number of issues' is plural, so 'is' should be 'are' or 'were'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'There is' is used with singular subjects; 'there are' is used with plural subjects.

rules.title: 1. There is + singular subject
rules.explanation: Use 'is' with singular or uncountable nouns.
rules.structure: There is + singular/uncountable noun
notes: There is a problem.
There is water on the floor.

rules.title: 2. There are + plural subject
rules.explanation: Use 'are' with plural nouns.
rules.structure: There are + plural noun
notes: There are a number of issues.
There are many reasons.

common_mistakes.wrong: There is a number of issues.
common_mistakes.correct: There are a number of issues.

other_examples.sentence: There are several options available.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'The pair' (singular), not 'scissors'. Therefore, the main verb should be 'belongs' or 'should belong'. The relative clause 'that were left' can agree with 'scissors', which is plural.
details_explanation.introduction: 'A pair of' makes a plural noun singular for agreement purposes.

rules.title: 1. A pair of + plural noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: The subject is 'pair'.
rules.structure: A pair of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: A pair of scissors is on the table.
The pair of shoes belongs to me.

rules.title: 2. Plural noun without 'pair'
rules.explanation: Without 'pair', two-part nouns are plural.
rules.structure: Scissors/pants/glasses + plural verb
notes: The scissors are sharp.
My glasses are broken.

common_mistakes.wrong: The pair of scissors belong to me.
common_mistakes.correct: The pair of scissors belongs to me.

other_examples.sentence: A pair of glasses is missing.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'The flock' (singular collective noun), so the verb should be 'has been flying' or 'was flying'. The phrase 'of geese' does not change the subject.
details_explanation.introduction: Collective nouns for animals, such as 'flock', 'herd', 'pack', and 'school', are singular when the group is viewed as a unit.

rules.title: 1. Collective noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: The group acts as one unit.
rules.structure: Collective noun + singular verb
notes: The flock has flown south.
A herd of cattle is grazing.

rules.title: 2. Subject is the collective noun
rules.explanation: The phrase 'of + plural noun' does not control the verb.
rules.structure: Collective noun + of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: The pack of wolves is hunting.
The school of fish is swimming.

common_mistakes.wrong: The flock of geese have flown south.
common_mistakes.correct: The flock of geese has flown south.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'The CEO' (singular). The phrase 'together with the board members' is an intervening phrase and does not make the subject plural. The verb should be 'has approved' or 'approved'.
details_explanation.introduction: Phrases such as 'together with', 'along with', 'as well as', and 'in addition to' do not compound the subject.

rules.title: 1. Together with does not create a plural subject
rules.explanation: The verb agrees with the first subject only.
rules.structure: Singular subject + together with + noun + singular verb
notes: The CEO together with the board has approved the plan.
The teacher together with the students is attending.

rules.title: 2. Difference from 'and'
rules.explanation: 'And' creates a compound subject; 'together with' does not.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 = plural; S1 together with S2 = agrees with S1
notes: The CEO and the board have approved.
The CEO together with the board has approved.

common_mistakes.wrong: The CEO together with the board have approved.
common_mistakes.correct: The CEO together with the board has approved.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Neither of' is singular and takes a singular verb, even when followed by a plural noun. The correct verb is 'seems' or 'appears'.
details_explanation.introduction: Indefinite pronouns 'neither' and 'either' are singular.

rules.title: 1. Neither of + plural noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: 'Neither' is the subject.
rules.structure: Neither of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: Neither of the solutions seems feasible.
Neither of the boys is here.

rules.title: 2. Either of + plural noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: 'Either' is also singular.
rules.structure: Either of + plural noun + singular verb

details_explanation.explanation: 'None of' can take a singular or plural verb depending on the noun after 'of'. Here, 'water' is uncountable/singular, so the verb should be 'has been wasted' or 'was wasted'.
details_explanation.introduction: With 'none of + uncountable noun', use a singular verb; with 'none of + plural noun', singular or plural verbs are often acceptable depending on meaning.

rules.title: 1. None of + uncountable noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: Uncountable nouns take singular verbs.
rules.structure: None of + uncountable noun + singular verb
notes: None of the water has been wasted.
None of the information was accurate.

rules.title: 2. None of + plural noun
rules.explanation: Both singular and plural verbs can be acceptable, but plural is common when referring to individual items.
rules.structure: None of + plural noun + singular/plural verb
notes: None of the students are absent.
None of the students is absent.

common_mistakes.correct: None of the water has been wasted.

details_explanation.introduction: Some nouns ending in -s are singular, including 'news', 'mathematics', 'physics', and 'economics' when referring to a field of study.

rules.title: 1. News is singular
rules.explanation: Use a singular verb with 'news'.
rules.structure: The news + singular verb
notes: The news is good.
The news has surprised everyone.

rules.title: 2. Academic subjects ending in -s

rules.structure: Mathematics/physics/economics + singular verb

details_explanation.explanation: Amounts of money, time, and distance are treated as singular units. 'Twenty dollars' takes a singular verb: 'is' or 'was'.
details_explanation.introduction: When a sum of money, a period of time, or a distance is viewed as a single unit, use a singular verb.

rules.title: 1. Money as a unit
rules.explanation: Use a singular verb with amounts of money.
rules.structure: Amount of money + singular verb
notes: Twenty dollars is too much.
Five hundred euros was stolen.

rules.title: 2. Time and distance
rules.explanation: Treat time and distance as singular units.
rules.structure: Amount of time/distance + singular verb
notes: Ten years is a long time.
Five miles is a long walk.

common_mistakes.wrong: Twenty dollars are too much.
common_mistakes.correct: Twenty dollars is too much.
common_mistakes.reason: The amount is treated as one unit.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Fish and chips' refers to one dish, so it is treated as singular and takes a singular verb: 'is' or 'was'.
details_explanation.introduction: When two nouns joined by 'and' refer to a single idea, dish, or person, the verb is singular.

rules.title: 1. Single dish or concept
rules.explanation: Compound subjects that refer to one entity take singular verbs.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 (one entity) + singular verb
notes: Fish and chips is a popular dish.
Bread and butter is delicious.

rules.title: 2. Two distinct items
rules.explanation: If the two nouns are separate, use a plural verb.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 (separate) + plural verb
notes: The fish and the chips are on separate plates.
The bread and the butter are on the table.

common_mistakes.wrong: Fish and chips are my favorite meal.
common_mistakes.correct: Fish and chips is my favorite meal.

details_explanation.explanation: Two distinct subjects joined by 'and' form a plural subject. The verb should be 'are collaborating' or 'collaborate'.
details_explanation.introduction: Compound subjects joined by 'and' take plural verbs unless they refer to a single entity.

rules.title: 1. S1 and S2 + plural verb
rules.explanation: Two separate subjects require a plural verb.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 + plural verb
notes: The teacher and the researcher are collaborating.
The cat and the dog are playing.

rules.title: 2. Exception: one entity
rules.explanation: If the two nouns refer to one person or idea, use a singular verb.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 (same entity) + singular verb
notes: My friend and colleague is here.
Bread and butter is delicious.

common_mistakes.wrong: The teacher and the researcher is collaborating.
common_mistakes.correct: The teacher and the researcher are collaborating.
common_mistakes.reason: Two subjects joined by 'and' are plural.

other_examples.sentence: The manager and the assistant are working late.
The sun and the moon are visible.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'The teacher' (singular). The phrase 'as well as the researchers' is an intervening phrase and does not change the subject. The verb should be 'is collaborating' or 'collaborates'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'As well as' does not compound the subject; it adds parenthetical information.

rules.title: 1. As well as does not create a plural subject
rules.explanation: The verb agrees with the first subject.
rules.structure: Singular subject + as well as + noun + singular verb
notes: The teacher as well as the researchers is collaborating.
The CEO as well as the managers was present.

rules.title: 2. Difference from 'and'
rules.explanation: 'And' makes a compound plural subject; 'as well as' does not.
rules.structure: S1 and S2 = plural; S1 as well as S2 = agrees with S1
notes: The teacher and the researchers are collaborating.
The teacher as well as the researchers is collaborating.

common_mistakes.wrong: The teacher as well as the researchers are collaborating.
common_mistakes.correct: The teacher as well as the researchers is collaborating.

other_examples.sentence: The manager, as well as the staff, is attending.
The children, as well as their parents, are excited.
other_examples.translation: Anak-anak, serta orang tua mereka, bersemangat.

details_explanation.explanation: In 'There is/are ...', the verb agrees with the noun phrase after it. 'A committee' is singular, so 'are' should be 'is' or 'was'.
details_explanation.introduction: The existential 'there' is not the subject; the noun following the verb determines agreement.

rules.title: 1. There is + singular noun
rules.explanation: Use 'is' with a singular noun.
rules.structure: There is + singular noun
notes: There is a committee.
There is a problem.

rules.title: 2. There are + plural noun
rules.explanation: Use 'are' with a plural noun.
rules.structure: There are + plural noun
notes: There are committees.
There are problems.

common_mistakes.wrong: There are a committee that oversees the budget.
common_mistakes.correct: There is a committee that oversees the budget.

other_examples.sentence: There is a team responsible for the project.
other_examples.translation: Ada tim yang bertanggung jawab atas proyek itu.

other_examples.sentence: There are several teams involved.

details_explanation.explanation: The subject is 'The number', which is singular. The relative clause 'who commute by bicycle' refers to 'people', but it does not change the number of the main subject. The verb should be 'has increased' or 'increased'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'The number of' takes a singular verb; relative clauses inside the noun phrase do not change the main subject.

rules.title: 1. Main subject is 'the number'
rules.explanation: Use a singular verb for the main clause.
rules.structure: The number of + plural noun + relative clause + singular verb
notes: The number of people who commute has increased.
The number of cars that were sold has risen.

rules.title: 2. Relative clause agrees with its antecedent
rules.explanation: Inside the relative clause, the verb agrees with the plural noun it refers to.
rules.structure: People who commute + plural verb
notes: People who commute by bicycle are healthier.
The people who work here are friendly.

common_mistakes.wrong: The number of people who commute have increased.
common_mistakes.correct: The number of people who commute has increased.

other_examples.sentence: The number of students who study abroad has grown.
other_examples.translation: Jumlah siswa yang belajar di luar negeri telah tumbuh.

other_examples.sentence: A number of students who study abroad have returned.
other_examples.translation: Sejumlah siswa yang belajar di luar negeri telah kembali.

references.title: The Number of and Relative Clauses
references.author: GrammarBook.com

details_explanation.explanation: In 'What the committee needs ...', the subject is the whole 'what' clause, which is treated as singular here. The complement 'a clearer policy' is singular, so the verb should be 'is' or 'would be'.
details_explanation.introduction: A 'what' clause as subject is usually singular when it refers to a single idea, amount, or thing.

rules.title: 1. What clause + singular verb
rules.explanation: Use a singular verb when the 'what' clause represents a single need or idea.
rules.structure: What + clause + singular verb + singular complement
notes: What the committee needs is a clearer policy.
What we need is more time.

rules.title: 2. Plural complement
rules.explanation: A plural verb is possible when the complement is plural and the focus is on multiple items.
rules.structure: What + clause + plural verb + plural complement
notes: What we need are clearer policies.
What the students want are better facilities.

common_mistakes.wrong: What the committee needs are a clearer policy.
common_mistakes.correct: What the committee needs is a clearer policy.
common_mistakes.reason: The complement 'a clearer policy' is singular.

other_examples.sentence: What the team needs is more practice.
other_examples.translation: Yang dibutuhkan tim adalah lebih banyak latihan.

other_examples.sentence: What we need are more resources.
other_examples.translation: Yang kita butuhkan adalah lebih banyak sumber daya.

details_explanation.explanation: 'Every one' is singular and takes a singular verb. The correct verb is 'has submitted' or 'submitted'.
details_explanation.introduction: 'Every one of' is different from 'everyone'. 'Every one' emphasizes each individual and is singular.

rules.title: 1. Every one of + plural noun + singular verb
rules.explanation: The subject is 'every one'.
rules.structure: Every one of + plural noun + singular verb
notes: Every one of the applicants has submitted.
Every one of the books is new.

rules.title: 2. Everyone is also singular
rules.explanation: 'Everyone' is a single indefinite pronoun.
rules.structure: Everyone + singular verb
notes: Everyone has submitted.
Everyone is ready.

common_mistakes.wrong: Every one of the applicants have submitted.
common_mistakes.correct: Every one of the applicants has submitted.

other_examples.sentence: Every one of the rooms has a view.
Everyone has finished the test.

details_explanation.explanation: Names of countries that are grammatically plural in form but singular in meaning, such as 'The United States', take singular verbs. The verb should be 'has announced' or 'announced'.
details_explanation.introduction: Some proper nouns ending in -s are treated as singular because they refer to one country, organization, or entity.

rules.title: 1. The United States is singular
rules.explanation: It refers to one country.
rules.structure: The United States + singular verb
notes: The United States has announced new tariffs.
The United States is a large country.

rules.title: 2. Similar singular proper nouns
rules.explanation: Other country names and organization names ending in -s may also be singular.
rules.structure: Singular entity + singular verb
notes: The Philippines is an archipelago.
The United Nations has a headquarters in New York.

common_mistakes.wrong: The United States have announced new tariffs.
common_mistakes.correct: The United States has announced new tariffs.
common_mistakes.reason: The country is treated as one singular entity.

other_examples.sentence: The United States has a new president.
The United Nations is meeting today.
other_examples.translation: Perserikatan Bangsa-Bangsa sedang rapat hari ini.
